Abstract
Objective  This study aims to differentiate between symptomatic and asymptomatic plaques using a computed 
tomography angiography (CTA)-based radiomics model of perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT).
Methods  Patients were categorized into symptomatic and asymptomatic groups based on the presence or absence 
of acute ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack in the anterior cerebral circulation within two weeks prior to the 
CTA examination. The clinical information of all patients was collected and analyzed, and the PVAT features of CTA 
images were further analyzed to clarify their correlation with plaque classification. K-nearest neighbors (KNN), support 
vector machine (SVM), logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), multinomial 
naive Bayes (MultinomialNB), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) were trained and radiomics (Rad) score 
was calculated using the best classifier. A combined model was further developed based on the Rad-score and 
independent predictors, and the calibration, receiver operating characteristic curve, decision curve analysis, and 
clinical applicability were evaluated.
Results  The white blood cell count and hyperlipidemia were clinically independent predictors, and ten PVAT 
radiomics features showed significant correlation. The XGBoost classifier showed the best performance among 
different classifiers, with an average AUC of 0.797 in the validation set. The combined model integrating Rad-score 
and clinically independent predictors was further obtained, with AUCs of 0.942, 0.797, and 0.836 in the training, 
external validation sets, respectively.
Conclusion  The combined model performed excellently in predicting symptomatic carotid plaques. By early 
identification of high-risk patients and selecting appropriate clinical decisions, it holds significant clinical potential for 
improving stroke prevention.

Introduction
Stroke is the second foremost cause of disability and 
mortality globally, causing millions of deaths annually [1, 
2]. The Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) predicts 
that by 2050, there will be more than 200 million stroke 
patients each year, including 25 million new stroke cases 
and 13 million stroke-related deaths [3]. Carotid athero­
sclerosis is an important cause of stroke, accounting for 
15–20% of ischemic stroke events [4, 5]. Compared to 
low-risk carotid plaques, high-risk carotid plaques are 
more prone to rupture, leading to the occurrence of isch­
emic stroke and often result in residual impairments in 
motor, sensory, speech, or cognitive functions [6], high­
lighting the importance of early prediction of symp­
tomatic plaques. Therefore, accurate carotid plaque risk 
assessment is crucial for personalized treatment plans to 
prevent stroke.
The underlying mechanisms of stroke caused by carotid 
atherosclerosis are complex and can be inferred from the 
characteristics of the plaques [7–9]. Studies have indi­
cated that the clinical outcome of atherosclerotic plaques, 
and whether they lead to ischemic stroke depends not 
only on the degree of luminal stenosis, but also on the 
specific composition characteristics of the plaques [10–
12]. In addition, the evaluation of various plaque char­
acteristics has received increasing attention, such as 
inflammation, thin fibrous caps, intraplaque hemorrhage, 
and lipid-rich cores [13, 14]. Among them, inflammation 
is the main factor in the formation and rupture of ath­
erosclerotic plaques [15–17]. Previous studies have found 
that inflammation in atherosclerotic plaques has a stable 
and long-term effect on the surrounding perivascular adi­
pose tissue (PVAT), and inflammatory cytokines released 
from a vessel wall undergoing atherosclerosis diffuse 
to PVAT in a paracrine fashion, inhibiting the differen­
tiation of preadipocytes and promoting lipid buildup 
[18, 19]. A previous study has reported that inflamma­
tion linked to high-risk carotid artery plaques could be 
evaluated through variations in PVAT density on CT 
images [20]. However, these changes, including fibrosis 
and changes in vascular distribution, cannot be accu­
rately reflected by simply measuring the CT values [21]. 
Instead, it is necessary to perform comprehensive feature 
extractions of the PVAT surrounding carotid plaques at a 
higher dimension to fully capture these changes, thereby 
enhancing the prediction of symptomatic plaques.
Radiomics, an emerging image analysis technique, 
allows for the high-throughput extraction of quantita­
tive features from medical images and ascertaining their 
patterns to provide clinical decision support [22, 23]. Ini­
tially applied in oncology, radiomics has gradually been 
used in predicting diseases associated with the coronary 
arteries [24–26]. Machine learning (ML) as an emerging 
tool is also widely used in research in the field of vas­
cular medicine [27, 28]. Recent research has confirmed 
the association between inflammation-induced attenua­
tion changes in coronary artery PVAT and the develop­
ment of coronary artery disease and vulnerable plaques 
[29]. However, to our knowledge, there appears to be a 
scarcity of research exploring the connection between 
inflammatory changes in the PVAT of carotid arter­
ies and cerebrovascular events [30, 31]. Moreover, these 
studies have only assessed the inflammation of carotid 
plaques based on the density of PVAT or were unable to 
investigate the entirety of PVAT due to technical limita­
tions. Hence, predicting symptomatic carotid plaques 
using radiomics combined with various ML algorithms 
remains uncharted territory.
This study aims to establish and test a radiomics model 
based on carotid perivascular PVAT to improve the accu­
racy of identifying high-risk carotid plaques, and to com­
pare the diagnostic value of various models, to better 
assist in the selection of clinical treatment plans.
Methods
Patient selection and classification
This study was approved by the institutional review 
board, and individual consent for this retrospective 
analysis was waived (No. 2024 − 508, the Fifth Affili­
ated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University).Clinical 
trial number: not applicable.Retrospective collection of 
imaging data from patients confirmed with carotid ath­
erosclerosis occurred at the Fifth Affiliated Hospital of 
Wenzhou Medical University (center 1) from January 
2018 to December 2023, the Second Affiliated Hospital 
of Wenzhou Medical University (center 2) and the Lishui 
People’s Hospital (center 3) from January 2022 to Decem­
ber 2023.Center 1 is used as the training set, and cen­
ters 2 and 3 are used as external validation sets 1 and 2, 
respectively. The inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria and 
collection of clinical data are detailed in Appendix E1 and 
Appendix E2. Subsequently, we categorized the selected 
patients.
Key points
1. Perivascular adipose tissue radiomics can predict symptomatic carotid artery plaques.
2. Combined model using radiomics and clinical predictors excels in identifying symptomatic plaques.
3. The nomogram accurately identifying high-risk carotid plaques will aid clinical decision-making.

Patients were classified as symptomatic or asymptom­
atic according to the results of a neurological assess­
ment following the TOAST criteria [32] and the results 
of a brain MRI plain scan. Patients with a transient isch­
emic attack (TIA) or acute ischemic stroke occurring in 
the area supplied by the carotid artery were considered 
symptomatic. Acute ischemic stroke was defined as neu­
rological deficits persisting for more than 24 h or neuro­
logical deficits accompanied by cranial MRI findings [33]. 
The MRI findings of acute ischemic stroke included high 
signal intensity lesions on diffusion-weighted imaging 
sequences and low signal intensity on apparent diffusion 
coefficient sequences. TIA was defined as a transient epi­
sode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain or 
retinal ischemia [33]. Patients without any TIA or stroke 
in the previous six months were classified as asymptom­
atic. A flowchart depicting the patient selection process 
is presented in Fig. 1.
Examination methods
All the CTA scans were performed on a 256-slice CT 
scanner. Additional information about the CTA param­
eters from three distinct centers can be found in Appen­
dix E3.
Image segmentation
All CTA images were uploaded to Radcloud platform 
(version 7.1, http://radcloud.cn/) for analysis. First, 
two radiologists (both with > 8 years of imaging experi­
ence) delineated the target vessels and the surrounding 
plaques on the CTA images. Then PVAT was defined as 
the adipose tissue located at a radial distance from the 
outer vessel wall equivalent to the diameter of the ves­
sel; its Hounsfield Unit (HU) values ranged from − 190 to 
− 30. The delineation of PVAT was performed automati­
cally by establishing a specific attenuation threshold. The 
length and coverage range of target vessels were the areas 
with plaques at the selected bifurcation of the carotid

sis according to NASCET criteria [34]. To reduce image 
heterogeneity, we preprocessed all the images (Appendix 
E4) before extracting radiomics features.
Radiomics features extraction and selection
A total of 1688 radiomics features (see in Appendix E5) 
were extracted from the PCAT surrounding plaques uti­
lized by Radcloud.
To evaluate the inter-reader reproducibility of 
radiomics features and ensure the robustness and stabil­
ity of our constructed models, we assessed the inter- and 
intra-class correlation coefficients (ICCs). (see in Appen­
dix E6). Features with ICC > 0.75 were selected for further 
analysis.
All radiomics features were standardized using the 
z-score algorithm to ensure that the scale of feature 
value was uniform and improved comparability between 
features. We employed a three-stage sequential feature 
selection process: First, we applied sequential analysis 
of variance (ANOVA) to eliminate features that did not 
show statistically significant group differences (p < 0.05 
after Holm-Bonferroni correction). Second, we used the 
SelectKBest univariate filter to retain the top 15% of fea­
tures. Finally, we applied the Least Absolute Shrinkage 
and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression to retain the 
most predictive features. An optimal lambda was selected 
through 10-fold stratified cross-validation. Features with 
non-zero coefficients in the model were considered the 
most representative.
Machine learning classifiers construction and evaluation
Then, we calculated the radiomics score for each patient 
by linearly combining the features with non-zero coeffi­
cients, weighted by their respective coefficients, and con­
structed seven machine learning classifiers. The selection 
of machine learning is detailed in Appendix E7. We 
employed the most common cross-validation method 
to check for overfitting or underfitting of the model. 
The evaluation of the prediction performance of the 
radiomics signatures included metrics such as the area 
under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve 
(AUC), specificity, sensitivity and accuracy (ACC). The 
radiomics model that exhibited the highest average AUC 
in the training set was chosen as the optimal radiomics 
model [35–37]. Then the results were transformed into a 
radiomics score (Rad-score).
Model and nomogram development and validation
We developed a total of four predictive models: the Ste­
nosis model, the Clinical model, the Radiomics model, 
and the Combined model. For the Stenosis model, we 
employed a logistic regression approach due to the lim­
ited number of input features. We conducted both uni­
variate and multivariate logistic regression analyses 
on the clinical characteristics of the symptomatic and 
asymptomatic groups in the training set to identify signif­
icant clinical predictive factors. Based on these findings, 
we formulated the Clinical model. Additionally, by inte­
grating Rad-scores with clinical features, we developed 
the Combined model and its corresponding nomogram 
through multivariable logistic regression analysis. We 
assessed the performance of all models using AUC, sen­
sitivity, specificity, and accuracy. Calibration curves were 
used to evaluate the agreement between observed out­
comes and predicted risks, and decision curve analysis 
(DCA) was used to determine the most beneficial model. 
Figure 2 illustrates a flowchart representing this research.
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were conducted by R software 
(version 
4.1.2, 
https://www.r-project.org/). 
Count 
data are presented as frequencies, and analyses com­
paring two groups were carried out utilizing either 
the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. Quantitative 
data that follow a normal distribution are expressed as 
mean ± standard deviation, with comparisons between 
groups executed through independent samples t-tests. 
For data that do not follow a normal distribution, medi­
ans (interquartile ranges) are provided, and the Wilcoxon 
test was employed for comparisons. The Pearson correla­
tion coefficient was used to calculate the degree of linear 
correlation between features. The DeLong test was used 
to assess the AUC between different models, and the 
associated P-value was calculated. A significance level of 
P < 0.05, two-tailed, was considered indicative of a mean­
ingful difference.
Results
Patient characteristics and clinical model construction
Our study comprised a total of 645 patients who under­
went carotid CTA. Among them, 232 patients were clas­
sified into the symptomatic group, while the remaining 
413 patients were categorized as asymptomatic. The 
clinical information is listed in Table  1. The difference 
in the degree of stenosis between the two patient groups 
was statistically significant in the training set (p = 0.041) 
but not in the validation sets (p > 0.05), potentially due 
to sample size limitations. Meanwhile, the clinical infor­
mation in training and validation sets show no statistical 
difference as displayed in Table S1. Based on the results 
of both univariate and multivariate regression analyses,

For the PVAT radiomic features, 192 features exhibiting 
an ICC < 0.75 were excluded. Among these excluded fea­

After excluding both intra-observer and inter-observer 
variability, we sequentially applied ANOVA, sequential 
analysis of variance, and LASSO regression to a total of 
1,496 features. This process resulted in the selection of 
495 features from ANOVA, 285 features from sequen­
tial analysis of variance, and ultimately 10 non-zero coef­
ficient features through LASSO regression. These 10 
selected features include 2 first-order statistical features, 
3 shape features, and 5 texture features, which were used 
for subsequent model development (Figure S1). Details 
regarding PVAT-related features within the symptomatic 
group can be found in Table S2 and the non-zero coef­

calculated, resulting in a correlation coefficient matrix 
heatmap represented in Fig. 3B.
Construction and evaluation of the ML classifiers
The specificity, sensitivity, accuracy, and AUC values of 
the ML classifiers as showed in Table  3 and Figure S2. 
The hyperparameter optimization of the seven machine 
learning classifiers is presented in Appendix E7. Within 
the training set, the AUC values for the classifiers var­
ied from 0.692 to 0.920, while the ACC ranged between 
57.99% and 88.42%. For the external validation sets, the 
average AUC values of the seven classifiers spanned from 
0.685 to 0.797, with the average ACC falling between 
65.37% and 76.53%. Among these classifiers, XGBoost 
performed the best, with average AUC values of 0.797, 
while the MultinomialNB classifier performed the worst 
with an AUC value of 0.685. Consequently, the XGBoost 
classifier was judged to be the most suitable machine 
learning algorithm for creating the radiomics model and 
used to calculate Rad-score. The ROC curves of the clas­
sifiers for the training and validation sets as showed in 
Figure S3. Detailed significance testing among the classi­
fiers can be found in Tables 4 and 5.

Discussion
Carotid atherosclerosis poses a risk for ischemic cerebro­
vascular events, making the early identification of symp­
tomatic carotid plaques and the selection of appropriate 
interventions or the development of surgical removal 
techniques crucial for stroke prevention. With deeper 
research into symptomatic plaques, their assessment 
through PVAT has become a focal point of study [38] 
and provides new insights into the formation of athero­
sclerotic plaques and the prediction of individual risks 
for ischemic stroke [20, 39]. However, traditional PVAT 
assessment methods have significant limitations in accu­
rately evaluating symptomatic plaques, primarily because 
they tend to focus only on changes in the CT values of 
PVAT and fail to fully capture the complex three-dimen­
sional structure of the adipose tissue [31, 40]. In this ret­
rospective study, we divided the patients into two groups 
based on whether they had experienced an acute isch­
emic stroke or a TIA in the anterior circulation: a symp­
tomatic group and an asymptomatic group. We then 
extracted the radiomic features of PVAT from multiple 
dimensions and established a predictive model based 
on these radiomic features to assess the risk of ischemic 
stroke in patients with carotid atherosclerosis. The model 
can classify patients into symptomatic and asymptomatic 
groups based on the Rad score and independent predic­
tive factors, thereby guiding clinical decision-making.
Vascular inflammation plays a crucial role not only in 
the development of atherosclerosis but also in influenc­
ing the transcriptional and structural changes of PVAT 
[18, 19]. These alterations manifest in CT images as an 
increase in the HU of PVAT, which correlates closely with 
plaque hemorrhage and ischemic symptoms [20, 41]. Si 
et al. [15] reported that plaque radiomics, combined with 
PVAT radiomics, can better differentiate patients with 
acute myocardial infarction from those with unstable 
angina. Oikonomou et al. [42] introduced a novel fat 
radiomics feature derived from PVAT radiomics obtained 
via coronary artery CTA and assessed its performance 
across three distinct patient cohorts, suggesting that fea­
tures based on PVAT radiomics are valuable for advanc­
ing risk assessments of adverse cardiac events. Zhang et 
al. [40] studied the average voxel intensity of the PVAT 
surrounding carotid artery plaques, which relied solely 
on CT attenuation to reflect changes in PVAT composi­
tion, without considering the complex spatial relation­
ship between voxels. Hence, this approach may lead to

of these independent predictors, this study established a 
clinical model. The clinical model showed moderate per­

the training and external validation sets, respectively. In 
order to improve the accuracy of predictions, we devel­
oped a combined model that integrates the Rad-score 
obtained from XGBoost along with the independent pre­
dictive variables discussed earlier. The findings revealed 
that the predictive efficacy of the combined model signif­

ing no significant difference in performance compared to 
the radiomics model. This limitation may stem from the 
study’s exclusive focus on the radiomic characteristics of 
PVAT without incorporating conventional imaging fea­
tures of the plaques. Future investigations that integrate 
plaque characteristics could potentially yield improved 
outcomes.
This research illustrates that PVAT may act as an imag­
ing biomarker for symptomatic plaques in the carotid 
artery and is closely associated with ischemic stroke. This 
finding provides a theoretical basis for the early preven­
tion of ischemic stroke. However, there were some limi­
tations in this study: (1) due to the retrospective nature 
of our study and the relatively small sample size, there 
may be selection bias in the patient selection process. 
The existing inclusion and exclusion criteria may not 
accurately represent the entire population. Therefore, 
future research should conduct rigorous large-scale pro­
spective studies to validate our findings and enhance 
the applicability of the model; (2) lack of histopathologi­
cal confirmation for PVAT inflammatory changes lim­
its direct pathological evidence; (3) we used traditional 
methods from coronary artery studies to measure PVAT. 
This difference may affect the accuracy of our assessment 
of PVAT in the context of carotid artery disease; (4) focus 
on maximally stenotic plaques could overlook high-risk 
non-stenotic lesions, warranting broader plaque assess­
ment in subsequent research; (5) the imbalance between 
the symptomatic and asymptomatic cohorts in our 
research may introduce bias into the model’s results. This 
discrepancy could raise questions about the robustness of 
the model and the presence of selection bias. To address 
this issue, our future cohort studies will implement strict 
balancing strategies to ensure that both symptomatic and 
asymptomatic patients are adequately represented.
Conclusions
In summary, this study established a predictive model 
for symptomatic carotid artery plaques by combining 
PVAT radiomics features with clinical characteristics 
and achieved satisfactory performance. Our model can 
provide important information for the development of 
clinical treatment strategies and serve as a reference for 
the selection of treatment strategies in high-risk carotid 
plaques.

Abstract: Objective This study aims to differentiate between symptomatic and asymptomatic plaques using a computed tomography angiography (CTA)-based radiomics model of perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT). Methods Patients were categorized into symptomatic and asymptomatic groups based on the presence or absence of acute ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack in the anterior cerebral circulation within two weeks prior to the CTA examination. The clinical information of all patients was collected and analyzed, and the PVAT features of CTA images were further analyzed to clarify their correlation with plaque classification. K-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), multinomial naive Bayes (MultinomialNB), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) were trained and radiomics (Rad) score was calculated using the best classifier. A combined model was further developed based on the Rad-score and independent predictors, and the calibration, receiver operating characteristic curve, decision curve analysis, and clinical applicability were evaluated. Results The white blood cell count and hyperlipidemia were clinically independent predictors, and ten PVAT radiomics features showed significant correlation. The XGBoost classifier showed the best performance among different classifiers, with an average AUC of 0.797 in the validation set. The combined model integrating Rad-score and clinically independent predictors was further obtained, with AUCs of 0.942, 0.797, and 0.836 in the training, external validation sets, respectively. Conclusion The combined model performed excellently in predicting symptomatic carotid plaques. By early identification of high-risk patients and selecting appropriate clinical decisions, it holds significant clinical potential for improving stroke prevention.
